first_impression.reaction: Sophie sent me this, so of course I'm reading it properly, top to bottom on the iPad. The opening is sensible and not gushing: 'Getting married in Italy as an Australian takes two documents, two countries and a sequence that has to run in the right order.' Good. That tells me it's serious. And I'm glad someone has said straight out that the British and American guides don't apply to us. The key takeaways box is the bit I'll screenshot for Geoff. My worry is that it's all about the couple's paperwork. Nothing yet about who is responsible if it goes wrong, and that's what I'm paying for.

journey.quote: Most guides online are written for British or American couples and talk about a Certificate of No Impediment, which Italy will not accept from you.
journey.reaction: Right, that's useful. Sophie had been reading an English website. This makes me think these people actually know the Australian side.

journey.section: Can Australians legally get married in Italy?
journey.quote: Rules change, so your Wedded Advisor confirms the current requirements for your date and comune.
journey.reaction: I like that someone checks. But who is this Advisor? A name would help. I want to know who I'd be ringing.

journey.section: What the Atto Notorio is and where to get it
journey.quote: In Sydney, both of you attend with four witnesses who are not related to either of you, though they can be related to each other.
journey.reaction: So Geoff and I can't be witnesses. Good to know now rather than at the consulate. Four unrelated adults is a lot to organise, though. I'd want someone to tell us whether the Melbourne rule is the same, since we're in Victoria.

journey.section: What the Atto Notorio is and where to get it
journey.quote: Melbourne books through the Prenot@mi portal and asks for proof of address in Victoria or Tasmania.
journey.reaction: Helpful that Melbourne is listed separately. 'Prenot@mi portal' means nothing to me, mind you. Is that a website? Will I have to help Sophie with it?

journey.section: What the Nulla Osta is and who signs it
journey.quote: Not published: how far ahead Rome and Milan release appointments, and whether a non-Australian partner attends. Your Wedded Advisor confirms both in writing before you book flights.
journey.reaction: I appreciate the honesty that it isn't published, and 'in writing' is exactly what I want to see. Flights for the whole family hang on this, so it matters.

journey.quote: At home, the order that works is certificate, then NAATI Italian translation, then a Notary Public's notarisation of the translation, then DFAT apostilles on the original and the translation.
journey.reaction: Clear order, but it's a lot of acronyms in one go. I followed it on the second read. Geoff will ask what a NAATI is.

journey.section: Step by step once you arrive in Italy
journey.quote: Rome's Prefettura legalisation office opens four mornings a week, and some comuni want your declaration three days before the wedding, so allow a working week rather than arriving two days out.
journey.reaction: This is the sort of practical advice I want. It also tells me the couple are running around Rome the week before the wedding while the rest of us are arriving. Who looks after the older relatives then?

journey.quote: Buy a revenue stamp (marca da bollo) at a tobacconist (tabaccaio) first.
journey.reaction: Very specific, which I like. But it does make me picture Sophie hunting for a tobacconist in Rome on her own. Does the Advisor do this, or do they?

journey.quote: Bagno a Ripoli does not provide one; finding the interpreter is up to you.
journey.reaction: Up to who, exactly? If we're paying a company to organise this, I'd expect them to find the interpreter. The page doesn't say whether they do. This is the bit that makes me nervous.

journey.section: Your timeline, working back from the wedding date
journey.quote: The squeeze is in the middle. Both documents expire six months after signing, so a date that moves late can mean signing again.
journey.reaction: Good warning, plainly put. The table is useful to print, though on the iPad I had to scroll sideways to read it.

journey.quote: Most official steps carry a fee, and amounts move with exchange rates or annual indexation.
journey.reaction: Then the list just says 'a fee applies' five times over. I understand they can't give exact figures, but even a rough range would help me budget. I do like that the Advisor 'costs the full paperwork in AUD'.

journey.quote: Not published: interpreter and translation rates. Your Wedded Advisor costs the full paperwork in AUD for your comune.
journey.reaction: AUD is good. That's what I want. But what does the Advisor themselves cost? Is that agreed in writing up front? Not a word about it.

journey.section: Plan the paperwork with one person
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor works in your time zone, quotes in AUD and stays with you from the first document to the last dance.
journey.reaction: 'Your time zone' and 'quotes in AUD' are the two most reassuring things on the page. 'The last dance' is a bit of sales talk, but I'll forgive it. Still no name, no phone number, and nothing about deposits or contracts.

unanswered_questions: Who is our Wedded Advisor, by name, and can I speak to them on the phone before anything is booked?
Who do we ring if something goes wrong in Italy, at night Italian time?
Does Wedded Wonderland book the Rome or Milan appointment, find the interpreter and handle the Prefettura, or does the couple do that themselves?
What does the Wedded Advisor service cost, and is that fee agreed in writing?
Are deposits paid to Italian venues and suppliers protected, and are contracts in English and in AUD?
Roughly how much does the paperwork come to in total, in AUD, even as a range?
Can older guests with limited mobility get into a town hall ceremony room, and is help arranged with transfers?
What travel or wedding insurance should we take out?

turn_offs_found.quote: Speak with a Wedded Advisor about your paperwork timeline
turn_offs_found.why: This is the first and only place the company really appears, and there is still no mention of contracts, deposits or who is responsible. That's the thing I need before I hand over money.

turn_offs_found.quote: Take both documents to the Ufficio Matrimoni (marriage office), with someone who can translate.
turn_offs_found.why: Lots of Italian terms in a row (comune, Prefettura, Ufficio Matrimoni, marca da bollo, tabaccaio, unione civile). They're explained, which is good, but by the middle I was flicking back to remember which office was which.

would_share_with: My husband Geoff, with my questions about cost and who is responsible
Sophie, to say we can't be her witnesses for the Atto Notorio

cta_reaction.quote: [Speak with a Wedded Advisor about your paperwork timeline](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge), starting with your date and your comune.
cta_reaction.why: 'Speak with' is what I want, if it really means a phone call with a person and not a form that goes nowhere. I'd click if it said I could book a call and named who I'd be talking to. I'd want to ask about fees, deposits and contracts before Sophie signs anything.

top_3_changes: Say plainly what the Wedded Advisor does and what the couple does themselves (booking the Rome or Milan appointment, finding the interpreter, the Prefettura). 'Finding the interpreter is up to you' made me wonder what we'd be paying for.

At the end, offer a phone call with a named person, and mention that fees are agreed in writing in AUD and who to contact if something goes wrong in Italy. A line about deposits and contracts would settle my biggest worry.

Add a short plain-English 'who's who' of the Italian offices (comune, Prefettura, Ufficio Matrimoni) and a rough AUD range for the paperwork, so a parent can follow along and budget without decoding each term.
